text.p: Lithuania's Vytautas Landsbergis, who on Monday claimed victory over his former communist foes in parliamentary elections, was the unlikely leader of the Baltic state's drive for independence from the former Soviet Union.

Landsbergis claimed victory after his Homeland Union Party unseated the ex-communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP) by becoming the largest group in parliament under a first round of elections.
It was a satisfying reversal for Landsbergis, who four years before had been rejected for the LDLP by a nation wearied by economic collapse and his independence movement's in-fighting.
The short and stocky former music professor was an unlikely leader but won the respect of many for himself and for ordinary Lithuanians as they confronted the former Soviet empire.

He refused to back down during the winter of 1991 when 13 people were killed in January during an attack by Soviet troops on the Vilnius television tower, a key point of resistance for the independence movement which was protected by ordinary people behind makeshift barricades.
Landsbergis came to prominence with his election as head of the Sajudis independence movement in 1988, when the nationalist cause was still in its infancy.
Sajudis took power in February 1990 and Landsbergis became head of parliament the following month.
Spurning the more gradualist approach of Estonia and Latvia, Lithuania set itself on a confrontation course with Moscow. The day Landsbergis was elected, parliament declared independence.
A furious Soviet leadership immediately threw up an economic blockade against Lithuania and the pressure caused Landsbergis to suspend the independence declaration and start negotiations.
With the Soviet Union paralysed by a coup attempt in August 1991, the Baltic states made the final break and declared their independence.
It was recognised by Moscow the following month.
But in the 1992 elections, voters snubbed Landsbergis for the familiar faces of the LDLP, the reformed communist party.
LDLP leader Algirdas Brazauskas sealed the party's comeback a year later by winning presidential elections.
True to his confrontational style, Landsbergis spent years after his defeat sniping at the LDLP, bitterly accusing them of corruption and being puppets of Moscow.
Political commentators expect him to take up the seat of speaker of parliament, in possible preparation for a fight for the presidency against Brazauskas in 1998.
Born on October 18, 1932, Landsbergis is the author of several books specialising in turn-of-the-century Lithuanian composer and artist Mikalojus Ciurlionis.
Landsbergis had impeccable family credentials to lead the Lithuanian revolution.

His father, a well-known architect, fought in the underground against the Nazis in World War Two. His grandfather, a journalist and playwright, was deported from the pre-revolutionary Russian empire for Lithuanian nationalism.
He is married with two daughters and a son.
